regulatory_context: (1) Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961: gives leagues an antitrust exemption to pool and sell national TV rights for 'sponsored telecasting' (free over-the-air); whether exclusive streaming packages are covered has been questioned, and members of Congress have raised concerns about games moving behind paywalls - a policy risk for an all-streaming NFL package. (2) NFL policy and local markets: NFL rules require games on streaming platforms to also air on local broadcast TV in the two team markets (as with Amazon's Thursday Night Football), which limits exclusivity. (3) FTC and DOJ scrutiny of media consolidation (the Warner Bros/Paramount fight) and of league-streamer deals; the 2024-25 Venu Sports joint venture (Disney/Fox/WBD) was blocked by a court injunction before being abandoned, showing antitrust appetite to police sports bundles. (4) Advertising: FTC rules on ad disclosure and children's privacy (COPPA) matter for live ad sales; state privacy laws (e.g. California CPRA) govern ad targeting on the ad tier. (5) Sports betting integrations: legal sports betting is state-regulated (about 38 states plus DC), so in-stream betting features would need state-by-state compliance. Overall: no hard barrier to Netflix bidding, but regulatory and political risk rises with full-season exclusivity. [uncertain] on current congressional proposals.

framework_applied: Product Strategy: Clarify, Context (4 pillars), Recommend (frameworks.md section 2); a strategic decision question ('should we do X'). Step 1 Clarify - define 'go big' (full-season packages such as an NFL or NBA package at $1-2 bn+ a year, versus more tentpole events), success (member acquisition and retention, ad revenue, engagement, brand), horizon (3-5 years), and constraints (content budget about $18-20 bn a year, margin targets, global vs US-only rights). Step 2 Context - Company positioning: the leading global streamer with high margins and an on-demand, global-first model; live is new, and the ad tier needs scarce, premium, live inventory; quick TAM check: US sports media rights about $30 bn a year, so 'going big' means a top-3 package at about $2-3 bn a year, which is about 10-15% of Netflix's content spend for a US-only product. Customers: core members want great stories; sports fans want every game of their team (season packages) and go where the games are; advertisers want live reach. Competition: Amazon (TNF, NBA, NASCAR), YouTube (Sunday Ticket, NFL game), Peacock (NBA, NFL, Sunday Night Baseball), ESPN DTC, Paramount+ (CBS NFL); substitutes are linear TV and highlights on social. Market forces: leagues hold the supplier power and rights inflate 5-10% a year; buyer (fan) churn is seasonal; threat of new entrants is high as tech firms bid; cost to enter is huge and recurring (rights expire, you build no lasting library). Step 3 Recommend - a reframe: 'Go big on live events, not on sports seasons' - own the biggest one-night moments, global and promotable rights, plus a few owned or long-term properties (WWE, boxing, women's sports), use them to power the ad tier and retention; avoid weekly full-season packages unless the price and global terms change; state the conditions under which the answer flips to yes.
clarifying_questions: Q: What does 'go big' mean - full-season packages (e.g. an NFL weekly package or NBA games) or more big events? A: The board is asking whether to bid for a full-season package when the NFL reopens its deals, roughly $2-3 bn a year.
Q: What is the goal - member growth, retention, ad revenue, or engagement? A: All matter, but the board cares most about revenue growth and operating margin. Ad revenue growth is a stated priority.
Q: Is this US-only or should I think about global rights? A: The question is about the US, but Netflix values rights that also work globally.
Q: What is the time horizon? A: Next 3-5 years; the next big NFL renegotiation could start as early as 2026-2027.
Q: Are there financial constraints? A: Content spend is about $18-20 bn a year and margins should keep expanding; a big package would need to fit inside that or justify a step-up.
Q: How have live events performed so far for acquisition and retention? A: I'll share data: sign-ups spike around events, retention after events is mixed.
Q: Is technical reliability a constraint? A: Early events (Paul vs Tyson, Nov 2024) had streaming issues; recent NFL games streamed smoothly.
interviewer_data_reveals: Exhibit 1 (real, Nielsen via AP) - Netflix NFL Christmas viewership: 2024 games about 24 mn US average each; 2025 Lions-Vikings 27.5 mn US (30.5 mn global), peaking above 30 mn; Cowboys-Commanders 22.4 mn global. Christmas Day 2025 set a 55.1 bn streaming-minutes record.

Exhibit 2 (real, widely reported) - Rights cost benchmarks: NFL 2021 deals about $110 bn over 11 years (about $10 bn a year across networks); Amazon Thursday Night Football about $1 bn a year; YouTube Sunday Ticket about $2 bn a year; NBA 11-year about $76 bn deal (Disney, NBC, Amazon) from 2025-26; Netflix WWE Raw about $500 mn a year; Netflix MLB about $50 mn a year.
Exhibit 3 (illustrative) - US sign-ups around live events, index normal week = 100: NFL Christmas week 240; major boxing night 210; WWE Raw weekly 115; MLB Opening Night 130.

Exhibit 4 (illustrative) - 6-month retention of members who joined in an event week vs a normal week: NFL Christmas joiners 58% vs 72% baseline; WWE Raw joiners 76%; boxing joiners 54%. Joiners who watched a scripted title in their first 14 days retain at 74% regardless of the event.

Exhibit 5 (illustrative) - Ad economics: live sports CPMs about 2-3x Netflix's on-demand ad CPMs; ad tier share of US sign-ups about 55-60%; a full NFL weekly package (17 games) would add about 2.5-3 bn ad impressions a season, worth about $0.9-1.2 bn in ad revenue at live CPMs.
Exhibit 6 (illustrative) - Viewing share: live sports are about 3% of Netflix US viewing hours in 2026, but about 25% of social media mentions of Netflix during event weeks.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Netflix has done NFL Christmas games, WWE Raw, boxing and MLB events. Should Netflix go big on live sports in the US?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: This is a 'should we' decision, so I'll clarify what 'go big' means and the goal, then look at Netflix's position, customers, competition and market forces, and give a recommendation with the conditions that would change it. Okay?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Go ahead.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: When we say 'go big', do we mean more events like Christmas games, or a full-season package - say a weekly NFL or NBA package?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: The board is asking whether to bid for a full-season package when the NFL reopens its deals - something like $2-3 billion a year.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: And the goal? Members, retention, ad revenue, or margin?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Revenue growth and operating margin matter most. Growing ads is a stated priority. Content spend is about $18-20 billion a year and margins should keep expanding.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: Got it - US question, but global rights are a plus, and a 3-5 year horizon. Let me start with Netflix's position. Netflix is the scale leader with over $51 billion in 2026 revenue and the best margins in streaming. Its model is on-demand, global-first storytelling: a show made once is watched in 190 countries for years. Live sports is the opposite: US-specific, watched once, and you rent it - when the rights end you keep nothing. The strength live gives is scarce, ad-friendly, appointment viewing, which the ad business needs: Netflix just cut its 2026 ad forecast to about $2.7 billion. So live is strategically useful, but the shape of the deal matters a lot.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Here's what we've seen. Exhibit 1: the 2025 Christmas Lions-Vikings game averaged 27.5 million US viewers, the most-streamed NFL game ever. Exhibit 2 gives rights costs.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: Quick sizing with Exhibit 2. The NFL collects about $10 billion a year from media. Amazon pays about $1 billion a year for Thursday Night Football, YouTube about $2 billion for Sunday Ticket. A Netflix full-season package at $2-3 billion a year would be about 10-15% of total content spend, for a product that mostly matters to US members - who are a minority of Netflix's global base. So the bar is: does it bring in enough incremental US revenue to pay for itself?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Who are the customers here?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text:
Three groups:
- Existing members: mostly there for series and films; a big game is a nice bonus and increases the feeling that Netflix is 'where culture happens'.
- Sports-first fans and cord-cutters: they follow a team, not a platform. They need every game, and they churn when the season ends. Their pain is fragmentation - NFL games are on CBS, Fox, NBC, ESPN, Amazon, YouTube and Peacock.
- Advertisers: their pain is that linear TV reach is shrinking and live sports are the last big reliable reach. They pay a premium.
Netflix's own pain is twofold: growth in US members is slowing because it's highly penetrated, and the ad tier needs premium inventory.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Exhibit 3: sign-ups in NFL Christmas week are 2.4x a normal week, boxing 2.1x, WWE Raw weeks 1.15x, MLB Opening Night 1.3x.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: Events clearly drive sign-ups. But the question is whether those members stay. Do you have retention?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Exhibit 4: six-month retention for NFL Christmas joiners is 58% versus a 72% baseline; WWE Raw joiners retain at 76%; boxing 54%. Joiners who watch a scripted title in their first 14 days retain at 74% regardless of the event.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text:
That's the key insight. One-off events bring trial, but people churn unless we convert them to our core product. Recurring weekly properties like WWE retain best because they create a habit. So a full NFL season would retain better than a single Christmas game - but only during the season, and seasonal churn is a known problem for sports streamers. Now competition:
| Player | Live sports position | Implication for Netflix |
| Amazon Prime Video | TNF, NBA, NASCAR, Black Friday game | Proves streaming can carry a weekly NFL package |
| YouTube | Sunday Ticket, NFL Brazil game | Biggest TV-time share; deep pockets |
| Peacock (NBC) | NBA, NFL, MLB Sunday Night Baseball | Uses sports to drive its subs |
| ESPN DTC / Fox One | Full sports catalogues | Sports-first destinations |
| Paramount+ | CBS NFL, UFC from 2026 | Now combined with Warner Bros |
Everyone else is buying sports because their on-demand libraries can't compete with Netflix's. Netflix doesn't need sports to survive - it can choose.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: What about market forces?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: Supplier power is the decisive force: leagues are monopolies on their content, and each renewal raises the price - NFL and NBA deals rose sharply in the last round. Buyer power, meaning fans, is moderate: they'll follow the games anywhere, but they churn after the season. Threat of entry is high - Apple, Amazon and YouTube all bid with money from other businesses, so prices aren't set by streaming economics. And the cost of entry is permanent: you don't build a library, and losing the renewal means losing the audience. Politically, the Sports Broadcasting Act and pressure about games behind paywalls also mean the NFL keeps local broadcast simulcasts, so we wouldn't even get full exclusivity.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Here are ad economics. Exhibit 5: live sports CPMs are 2-3x our on-demand CPMs. A weekly NFL package would add about 2.5-3 billion impressions a season, worth about $0.9-1.2 billion in ad revenue.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text:
Let me do the full-season math, illustratively:
| Line item | Annual estimate |
| Rights cost | -$2.5 bn |
| Production and tech | -$0.3 bn |
| Ad revenue at live CPMs | +$1.0 bn |
| Incremental members retained (about 3 mn US at about $15/month net) | +$0.5 bn |
| Reduced churn among existing members (about 0.2 pts) | +$0.3 bn |
| Net | about -$1.0 bn a year |
So a full NFL weekly package likely loses about $1 billion a year on direct economics, before brand value. Compare the Christmas package: a few games for a fraction of the cost, with massive reach and global attention. Event economics are much better than season economics.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: But sports are 25% of social chatter during event weeks even though they're only 3% of viewing hours (Exhibit 6). Isn't that worth paying for?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: It is - and it's exactly why events work. Netflix gets the cultural moment without paying for 17 weeks of regular-season games that compete with Sunday afternoon on CBS and Fox. The marginal hour of a regular-season game is worth much less than Christmas night.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: So what's your recommendation?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text:
My recommendation is a reframe: Netflix should go big on live events, not on sports seasons. Concretely:
1. Own the biggest one-night moments: NFL holidays (Christmas, Thanksgiving Eve), MLB Opening Night and the Home Run Derby, big boxing and combat nights, the FIFA Women's World Cup - each a single promotable night that's 'only on Netflix'.
2. Hold a few weekly, habit-forming properties where Netflix has scale or long-term control: WWE Raw is the model - long contract, global rights, scripted-like storytelling, strong retention.
3. Prefer global rights and properties that travel, plus rising categories like women's sports, where prices are still reasonable.
4. Wrap every event in the Netflix flywheel: docuseries like 'Quarterback' and 'Full Swing' before and after, and in-app recommendations that move event joiners into scripted titles within 14 days.
5. Use live inventory to power the ad tier: premium CPM packages sold with on-demand inventory.
And don't bid for a full-season NFL or NBA package at $2-3 billion a year on today's terms.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Under what conditions would you change your mind and bid?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: Three triggers. (1) Global rights: if the NFL offers a package with worldwide streaming rights - for example, the international game slate plus a US window - the value per dollar improves a lot. (2) Ad tier maturity: if Netflix's ad tech gets live CPMs and fill rates where the ad line covers at least 60-70% of the rights cost. (3) Competitive threat: if YouTube or Amazon start using sports to win significant share of US TV time from Netflix, defending engagement might justify the loss. If two of these three hold, I'd bid for a mid-size package - say a weekly window of about $1-1.5 billion - not the biggest one.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: What risks do you accept by not going big?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: Two main ones. First, we could lose the 'TV of record' position to YouTube, which already has the biggest share of US TV time. Mitigation: keep owning the biggest single nights plus WWE, and keep our on-demand lead. Second, leagues might shift their best events to partners who also buy full seasons. Mitigation: be the best partner for events - global reach, flawless streaming, promotion and docuseries - which leagues value; MLB's deal shows they'll sell events to Netflix separately. For the events strategy itself, the risks are streaming failures, like the Paul vs Tyson issues, and the Sports Broadcasting Act politics, which we manage by keeping local broadcast simulcasts where required.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: How would you measure whether the events strategy is working?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: North Star: incremental retained members per live dollar - members who joined or were saved by an event and are still active six months later. Supporting metrics: event-week sign-ups, 14-day conversion of event joiners to scripted titles, live ad revenue and CPM, and share of US TV time. Guardrails: content cost growth versus revenue growth, overall operating margin, streaming quality (rebuffering, start failures) during live events, and churn after events.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: To sum up: live sports are valuable to Netflix for cultural moments, ads and retention - but full-season rights are a rented, inflating, US-only cost that destroys the economics of a global storytelling company. So yes to big live, no to big seasons: own the nights, own a few habits like WWE, sell premium ads on them, and turn every event joiner into a long-term member. We bid for a season only if the NFL brings global rights and our ad business can carry most of the bill.

answer_and_recommendation: Decision: No to a full-season package at $2-3 bn a year on current terms; yes to scaling live events. Reframe: 'Go big on live events, not on sports seasons.' Ranked options: (1) Tentpole events - NFL holidays (Christmas, Thanksgiving Eve), MLB Opening Night and Home Run Derby, big boxing/combat nights, FIFA Women's World Cup; best cost per cultural moment and sign-up spikes (illustrative 2.4x in NFL Christmas week; real 27.5 mn US viewers for Lions-Vikings 2025). (2) A few weekly habit-forming properties with long terms and global rights, modelled on WWE Raw (about $500 mn a year, illustrative 76% six-month retention of joiners). (3) Full-season NFL/NBA package - only if triggers are met. Why: illustrative season math shows about -$1 bn a year (rights $2.5 bn + production $0.3 bn vs ads $1.0 bn + new members $0.5 bn + churn savings $0.3 bn), rights are rented and inflating, mostly US-only, and the NFL still keeps local broadcast simulcasts. Execution: wrap events in docuseries and in-app recommendations to move joiners into scripted titles within 14 days; sell live inventory as premium ad packages; invest in live-streaming reliability. Conditions that flip the answer: global rights included, live ads covering 60-70% of rights cost, or YouTube/Amazon using sports to take meaningful US TV share - if two of three hold, bid for a mid-size weekly window (about $1-1.5 bn a year). Risks: losing 'TV of record' status to YouTube (mitigate by owning the biggest nights and the on-demand lead), leagues bundling events with seasons (mitigate by being the best global event partner), stream failures and paywall politics. Closing line: 'Yes to big live, no to big seasons - own the nights, own a few habits, and bid for a season only when the NFL brings global rights and our ad business can carry the bill.'
counter_metrics_guardrails: Guardrails: (1) operating margin and content cost growth vs revenue growth (live spend must not erode margin expansion); (2) six-month retention of event joiners vs baseline (target closing the gap from illustrative 58% to about 70%); (3) streaming quality during live events - start failures, rebuffering ratio, concurrent-stream capacity (Paul vs Tyson lesson); (4) post-event and post-season churn; (5) on-demand engagement per member (live must not crowd out scripted investment or the home page); (6) ad tier experience - ad load per live hour, ad complaints, ad tier NPS; (7) non-US member satisfaction and viewing (US-only rights should not reduce global content value); (8) cost per incremental retained member versus marketing-based acquisition cost.
follow_up_twists: Twist: 'YouTube just won a bigger NFL package and its US TV share keeps rising - does that change your answer?' Response: It moves the third trigger closer; I'd respond first by securing more NFL tentpole nights and a global international-games deal, and only bid on a weekly window if Netflix's share of US TV time actually declines.

Twist: 'The NFL offers worldwide rights to a weekly package at $2 bn a year.' Response: That meets the global trigger; re-run the math with international ad and member value - if live ads plus global retention cover about 70% of the cost, bid for it, ideally as a 5-year deal with flexibility.

Twist: 'Should Netflix just buy a league or a rights owner, like WWE's parent did with UFC?' Response: Owning IP is the only way to avoid rented, inflating rights; look for undervalued, story-rich properties (women's sports, combat sports, new leagues) where Netflix can grow the asset, not mature leagues priced for monopoly.
common_pitfalls: Answering a flat 'yes' because of record NFL viewership, without checking retention of event joiners and the cost of rented, inflating rights.
Treating all live as the same: a one-night event, a weekly entertainment property (WWE) and a 17-week season have very different economics and retention profiles.
Ignoring that Netflix is a global company - US-only rights cost global margin, while competitors (Amazon, YouTube, Apple) buy sports with money from other businesses.
Giving a 'no' without an alternative or conditions; strong answers reframe ('live events, not seasons') and state the triggers that would flip the decision.
skills_tested: business sense, structuring, quant, prioritisation, communication
